paragraphs: To keep the people from seeing too clearly what this arrangement would lead to, Servius tried to give it a military look. In the second class he placed two centuries of armorers, and in the fourth two of makers of weapons. In every class except the last he separated young and old, that is, those obliged to bear arms from those whose age legally exempted them. This distinction, more than that of wealth, made it necessary to repeat the census, or counting, often. Finally, he ordered the assembly to be held in the Campus Martius, and everyone of an age to serve to come there armed.

He did not make this division of young and old in the last class as well because the common people who composed it were not granted the right to bear arms for their country. A man had to own a hearth to acquire the right to defend it. Of all the troops of beggars who today lend luster to the armies of kings, there is perhaps not one who would not have been driven with scorn out of a Roman cohort, in the days when soldiers were the defenders of liberty.

Within this last class, though, _proletarians_ were set apart from _capite censi._ The proletarians were not quite reduced to nothing: they at least gave the State citizens, and at times of pressing need even soldiers. Those who had nothing at all, and could be counted only by heads, were considered worth nothing whatever. Marius was the first to stoop to enlisting them.

I will not now decide whether this third arrangement was good or bad in itself. But I think I can say that it could work only because the early Romans had simple morals, freedom from self-seeking, a love of farming, and a scorn for trade and for the love of gain. Where is the modern people among whom devouring greed, restlessness, intrigue, constant moves and endless swings of fortune would let such a system last twenty years without turning the State upside down? We must also note that at Rome morality and the censorship, which were stronger than this institution, corrected its faults, and that a rich man found himself demoted to the class of the poor for making too much display of his wealth.

All this makes it easy to see why people almost always mention only five classes, even though there were really six. The sixth supplied no soldiers to the army and no votes in the Campus Martius,[1] and it had almost no function in the State, so it was rarely thought to matter.

These, then, were the ways the Roman people was divided. Now let us look at how this affected the assemblies. A lawfully summoned assembly was called a _comitia_. Comitia usually met in the public square at Rome or in the Campus Martius, and they went by the names _Comitia Curiata, Comitia Centuriata_, and _Comitia Tributa_, depending on the form in which they were called together. Romulus founded the _Comitia Curiata_, Servius the _Centuriata_, and the tribunes of the people the _Tributa_. No law was approved and no magistrate elected anywhere but in the comitia. Every citizen was enrolled in a _curia_, a century or a tribe, so no citizen was shut out of the vote, and the Roman people was truly sovereign both _de jure_ and _de facto_.

Three conditions had to be met before the comitia could lawfully assemble and their acts have the force of law. First, the body or magistrate calling them needed the proper authority. Second, the meeting had to fall on a day the law allowed. Third, the auguries had to be favorable.

The reason for the first rule needs no explaining. The second is a matter of policy. For example, the comitia could not be held on festivals or market days, when country people came to Rome on business and had no time to spend the day in the public square. Through the third, the senate held the proud, restless people in check and properly restrained the ardor of seditious tribunes, who nonetheless found more than one way around this obstacle.

The comitia did not only vote on laws and elect rulers. The Roman people had taken the most important functions of government into its own hands, so one can say that the fate of Europe was settled in its assemblies. Because their business varied so much, the assemblies took different forms, depending on what they had to decide.

To judge these various forms, it is enough to compare them. When Romulus set up the _curiæ_, he meant the people to check the senate and the senate to check the people, while he kept his own ascendancy over both. So through this assembly he gave the people all the authority of numbers, to balance the power and riches he left to the patricians. But in keeping with the spirit of monarchy, he still left the patricians a greater advantage, in the influence their clients had on the majority of votes. This excellent institution of patron and client was a masterpiece of statesmanship and humanity. Without it the patriciate, which flatly contradicted the republican spirit, could not have survived. Rome alone has the honor of having given the world this great example, which never led to any abuse and yet has never been followed.
Under the kings the assemblies by _curiæ_ continued until Servius, and since the reign of the later Tarquin was not regarded as legitimate, royal laws were commonly called _leges curiatæ_.

Under the Republic the _curiæ_ stayed limited to the four urban tribes and held only the populace of Rome. They pleased neither the senate, which led the patricians, nor the tribunes, who, plebeians though they were, led the well-to-do citizens. They therefore lost standing, and fell so low that thirty lictors would meet and do the work the _Comitia Curiata_ ought to have done.

The division by centuries favored the aristocracy so strongly that at first it is hard to see how the senate could ever have lost in the comitia named after the centuries, the ones that elected the consuls, the censors and the other curule magistrates. The six classes of the whole Roman people were divided into a hundred and ninety-three centuries, and the first class held ninety-eight of them. Votes were counted by centuries alone, so this class by itself outvoted all the rest. When all its centuries agreed, the other votes were not even taken: the choice of the smallest number stood as the choice of the multitude. One may say that in the _Comitia Centuriata_ decisions were governed far more by the depth of purses than by the number of votes.

Two things, however, tempered this extreme power. First, the tribunes, as a rule, and a great many plebeians always belonged to the class of the rich, and they offset the influence of the patricians in the first class.

The second way was this. The centuries were not made to vote straight through in order, which would always have meant starting with the first. Instead the Romans always picked one by lot, and it voted alone. Then on another day all the centuries were summoned in order of rank, the same election was repeated, and as a rule confirmed. In this way the authority of example was taken away from rank and given to the lot, on a democratic principle.
